items.prompt: `OrderService.placeOrder()` mixes 15 lines of business rules with 25 lines of SQL client and Express plumbing in one function. Why does testing the business rules require Docker and a live database?
choices: Because business rules are inherently slow to test
Because the rule and the database call live in the same function with no seam between them — the rule can't run without dragging the infrastructure along
Because unit tests always need a real database for accuracy
This is unrelated to how the function is written
items.explanation: There's no separation enforcing 'rule' vs. 'infrastructure' inside a single tangled function — calling the rule means calling everything else in that function too, including the database client.
items.reference:
🐘 Real Postgres: ≈45ms/test
⚡ In-memory fake: ≈0.05ms/test

Why: a business rule tested through a port can be tested against a fake, in microseconds, with no infra.

items.reference:
🐘 Real Postgres: ≈45ms/test
⚡ In-memory fake: ≈0.05ms/test

Why: a business rule tested through a port can be tested against a fake, in microseconds, with no infra.

items.prompt: What's the actual cost being paid when business logic and infrastructure calls share the same function, beyond slower tests?
choices: Nothing else — it's purely a testing speed issue
Both testability AND the ability to change one side (say, swap databases) without touching the other — the coupling runs in both directions
Only code readability, not testability or swappability
It only matters for very large codebases
items.explanation: The coupling cuts both ways: it's not just that tests are slow, it's that changing the database technology also means editing the same function that holds the business rule, and vice versa.
items.reference:
🐘 Real Postgres: ≈45ms/test
⚡ In-memory fake: ≈0.05ms/test

Why: a business rule tested through a port can be tested against a fake, in microseconds, with no infra.

items.prompt: What's the difference between a port and an adapter?
choices: They're two names for the same thing
A port is an interface the core defines ('something that can save an order'); an adapter is a concrete implementation of that interface (Postgres, in-memory, etc.)
A port is always about HTTP; an adapter is always about databases
A port is written by the database team; an adapter is written by the core team
items.explanation: A port names a capability the core needs, in the core's own vocabulary, without saying how. An adapter is one specific way of fulfilling that capability — the core can be handed any adapter that honors the port.
items.reference:
Port

Interface the core defines and depends on

Adapter

Concrete class implementing a port

Why: the core names the port; adapters conform to it — never the other way around.

items.prompt: Which of these is a port, and which is an adapter: 'something that can save an order' vs. 'a class that saves an order into Postgres using the pg driver'?
choices: Both are ports
'Something that can save an order' is the port; the Postgres-specific class is the adapter implementing it
Both are adapters
The Postgres class is the port; the abstract description is the adapter
items.explanation: The abstract capability, described without naming a technology, is the port. The concrete, technology-specific class that fulfills it is the adapter — one port can have many adapters.
items.reference:
Port

Interface the core defines and depends on

Adapter

Concrete class implementing a port

Why: the core names the port; adapters conform to it — never the other way around.

items.prompt: A codebase has an `OrderRepository` interface with a `save()` method, and two classes implementing it: `PostgresOrderRepository` and `InMemoryOrderRepository`. How many ports and how many adapters is that?
choices: One port, two adapters
Two ports, one adapter
Three ports
Zero ports — interfaces don't count as ports
items.explanation: `OrderRepository` is the single port (the interface). `PostgresOrderRepository` and `InMemoryOrderRepository` are two separate adapters, each a distinct implementation of that same port.
items.reference:
Port

Interface the core defines and depends on

Adapter

Concrete class implementing a port

Why: the core names the port; adapters conform to it — never the other way around.

items.prompt: In ports & adapters, which direction do dependencies point?
choices: Outward — the core imports whichever adapter it needs directly
Inward, always — adapters depend on the core's port interfaces; the core never imports an adapter, a framework, or a driver
It varies per project, with no fixed rule
Adapters and the core depend on each other equally, in both directions
items.explanation: The one rule that makes the pattern work is that every dependency arrow points inward, toward the core. Adapters know about the core's ports; the core never knows about any specific adapter.
items.reference:
Adapter→Port←Core

Why: the core never imports an adapter or a framework — every dependency arrow points inward, toward the core's own port interfaces.

items.prompt: You find `import { Pool } from "pg"` inside a file that also contains the pricing calculation logic. What does that tell you about this codebase's dependency direction?
choices: Nothing unusual — pricing logic often needs a database import
The dependency direction has been violated — the core-level pricing logic now depends on a specific database driver instead of only depending on a port
This is fine as long as the import is at the top of the file
This only matters if the file is very large
items.explanation: A framework or driver import inside logic that's supposed to be core-level business logic is exactly the violation the pattern exists to prevent — the core is meant to depend only on ports it defines, never on `pg`, `express`, or similar packages directly.
items.reference:
Adapter→Port←Core

Why: the core never imports an adapter or a framework — every dependency arrow points inward, toward the core's own port interfaces.

items.prompt: Why does 'dependencies point inward' matter more than just 'keep files organized into folders named core/ and adapters/'?
choices: It doesn't — folder names alone are sufficient
Because folder structure is cosmetic; what actually enforces the boundary is which files' code imports which other files' code, regardless of folder name
Folder structure is the only thing that matters, imports are irrelevant
Both are equally irrelevant as long as tests pass
items.explanation: A file can sit in a folder called `core/` and still import a database driver directly — the folder name doesn't stop that. What actually enforces the boundary is the real dependency graph: which modules import which.
items.reference:
Adapter→Port←Core

Why: the core never imports an adapter or a framework — every dependency arrow points inward, toward the core's own port interfaces.

items.prompt: 'Hexagonal architecture' and 'clean architecture' — how do these two names relate to each other?
choices: They describe two competing, incompatible patterns
Different vocabulary for essentially the same underlying idea: business logic that doesn't depend on infrastructure or frameworks
Hexagonal is for backend systems only; clean architecture is for frontend only
Clean architecture replaced hexagonal architecture as an updated, unrelated pattern
items.explanation: Cockburn's hexagonal architecture (ports & adapters) and Martin's clean architecture use different terms — hexagon vs. concentric circles, port vs. boundary — but both enforce the same rule: the core doesn't depend on infrastructure.
items.reference:
⬡ Hexagonal (Cockburn) — core / ports / adapters
🏛️ Clean architecture (Martin) — use cases / entities / boundaries

Why: different vocabulary, same rule: business logic doesn't depend on infrastructure.

items.prompt: Why does this unit treat 'hexagonal architecture' and 'clean architecture' as one pattern instead of teaching them separately?
choices: Because there's no real overlap and grouping them is just for convenience
Because the core mechanism — a port the core defines, adapters that implement it, dependencies always pointing inward — is identical under both names
Because clean architecture doesn't actually use interfaces
Because hexagonal architecture doesn't apply to web applications
items.explanation: Both names describe the same mechanism: an application core with no outward dependencies, ports it defines, and adapters that implement those ports. The vocabulary differs; the dependency rule doesn't.
items.reference:
⬡ Hexagonal (Cockburn) — core / ports / adapters
🏛️ Clean architecture (Martin) — use cases / entities / boundaries

Why: different vocabulary, same rule: business logic doesn't depend on infrastructure.

choices: About twice as fast
Roughly 900x faster (about 45ms vs. about 0.05ms per test) — because the in-memory adapter does no network or disk I/O at all
There's no real difference once the database is warmed up

items.explanation: 45ms vs. 0.05ms is roughly a 900x difference — the in-memory adapter skips network round-trips and disk I/O entirely, since it's just an in-process data structure.

🐘 Real Postgres: ≈45ms/test
⚡ In-memory fake: ≈0.05ms/test

Why: a business rule tested through a port can be tested against a fake, in microseconds, with no infra.

items.prompt: What specifically makes it possible to swap in a fast in-memory adapter for tests, without the business rule 'knowing' anything changed?
choices: The business rule is rewritten specifically for the test environment
The business rule depends only on the port's interface, not on which adapter is plugged in — so any adapter honoring that interface works identically from the rule's point of view
In-memory adapters are always automatically substituted by the test framework
It isn't actually possible without changing the rule's code
items.explanation: Because the rule was written against the port's interface rather than a specific adapter class, any adapter satisfying that interface is interchangeable from the rule's perspective — including a fast in-memory one built purely for tests.
items.reference:
🐘 Real Postgres: ≈45ms/test
⚡ In-memory fake: ≈0.05ms/test

Why: a business rule tested through a port can be tested against a fake, in microseconds, with no infra.

items.prompt: In the hexagon diagram, solid arrows go from the core's use cases to its port interfaces, and dotted arrows go from each adapter back to that same port. What does the dotted-vs-solid distinction represent?
choices: Solid arrows mean 'faster'; dotted arrows mean 'slower'
Solid arrows are the core depending on a port it owns; dotted arrows are adapters implementing that port — two different relationships (depends-on vs. implements) drawn differently on purpose
There's no meaningful difference; it's just a stylistic choice
Dotted arrows mean the connection is optional and can be removed
items.explanation: The solid line is the core's real dependency — it depends on the port interface it owns. The dotted line is an adapter's promise to implement that interface. Distinguishing them makes explicit that the core never depends on any specific adapter.
items.reference:
Adapter→Port←Core

Why: the core never imports an adapter or a framework — every dependency arrow points inward, toward the core's own port interfaces.

items.prompt: Why isn't the number of sides on the 'hexagon' actually meaningful?
choices: It is meaningful — six sides map to exactly six required adapters
Cockburn picked hexagon just to have enough sides to draw several adapters around a core without implying a front/back the way a layered box diagram does — the shape is incidental, not a rule
The hexagon must always have exactly one primary and one secondary adapter per side
Six sides represent the six SOLID principles
items.explanation: The hexagon shape has no technical significance — it was chosen simply because it has enough sides to fit several adapters drawn around a core, unlike a layered rectangle which implies a top-to-bottom or front-to-back order that this pattern doesn't have.
items.reference:
Adapter→Port←Core

Why: the core never imports an adapter or a framework — every dependency arrow points inward, toward the core's own port interfaces.

items.prompt: Looking at the hexagon diagram, how would you tell, just from the arrows, whether the Postgres adapter or the core 'owns' the `OrderRepository` port's method signatures?
choices: You can't tell from the diagram at all

The core draws a solid dependency arrow to the port; the Postgres adapter only draws a dotted 'implements' arrow toward it — the side that depends-on (not implements) the interface is the one that defined it
Whichever box is drawn larger owns the interface
The adapter always owns the port's signatures, regardless of arrow direction
items.explanation: Ownership follows the solid dependency arrow: the core depends on (and therefore defines) the port. The adapter's dotted 'implements' arrow means it conforms to a shape it didn't get to choose.
items.reference:
Adapter→Port←Core

Why: the core never imports an adapter or a framework — every dependency arrow points inward, toward the core's own port interfaces.

items.prompt: A background worker consumes messages from a queue and calls `placeOrder()` for each one. Is that a primary or secondary adapter?
choices: Secondary, because a message queue is infrastructure
Primary — it calls INTO the core, the same as an HTTP controller does, just triggered by a message instead of a request
Neither — queue consumers aren't adapters at all
It depends only on which programming language it's written in
items.explanation: The direction of the call decides the category, not how infrastructure-flavored the trigger sounds. Since the worker calls into the core, it's a primary (driving) adapter, exactly like an HTTP controller or CLI command.
items.reference:
Primary (driving)

Calls INTO the core

Secondary (driven)

Called BY the core, through a port

Why: the direction of the call decides the category, not how infrastructure-y the technology sounds.

items.prompt: Why does it matter whether an adapter is classified as primary or secondary, beyond just naming?
choices: It doesn't matter in practice — the labels are purely decorative

Because the two kinds are tested differently: a primary adapter's test checks 'did I correctly translate an external trigger into a call on the core,' while a secondary adapter's test checks 'did I correctly implement the port's contract'
Only secondary adapters can be swapped; primary adapters are permanent
Primary adapters are always faster than secondary adapters
items.explanation: The classification changes what a correct test for that adapter even means — checking 'did I translate the trigger correctly' is a different question from 'did I implement the contract correctly,' and conflating them tests the wrong thing.
items.reference:
Primary (driving)

Calls INTO the core

Secondary (driven)

Called BY the core, through a port

Why: the direction of the call decides the category, not how infrastructure-y the technology sounds.

items.prompt: An email-sending class is called by the core through a `Notifier` port whenever an order ships. Is that primary or secondary?
choices: Primary, because sending email is user-facing
Secondary — the core calls it through a port the core defined; it never initiates a call into the core
It can't be classified without knowing which email provider is used
Primary, because email adapters always trigger further core logic
items.explanation: It's secondary: the core is the one initiating the call, through a port it owns (`Notifier`). The email adapter never calls into the core on its own — that's the defining trait of a secondary (driven) adapter.
items.reference:
Primary (driving)

Calls INTO the core

Secondary (driven)

Called BY the core, through a port

Why: the direction of the call decides the category, not how infrastructure-y the technology sounds.

items.prompt: Who is supposed to define the method signatures of a port like `OrderRepository`?
choices: Whichever team builds the database adapter, since they know the technology best
The core — always. A port's shape is written in the vocabulary of the business rule that uses it, not in the vocabulary of whatever will eventually implement it
Whichever adapter gets built first
It doesn't matter who defines it as long as it compiles
items.explanation: The core owns every port it depends on. If a port's shape were dictated by an adapter's convenience (say, a raw SQL fragment as a parameter), the dependency would have effectively flipped even if the diagram's arrow still points the 'right' way.
items.reference:
✓ Port shape: written in the core's vocabulary
✗ Port shape dictated by an adapter's convenience

Why: if a port's shape depends on how one adapter works, the dependency has quietly flipped even though the arrow on the diagram still points inward.

items.prompt: A port's `save()` method takes a raw SQL `WHERE` clause as a string parameter. What does that suggest went wrong?
choices: Nothing — that's a normal, well-designed port
The port's shape was dictated by what's convenient for a SQL database instead of by what the core actually needs — an honest in-memory adapter couldn't satisfy it without embedding a SQL interpreter
The port is fine, but only Postgres can implement it correctly
This only matters if the codebase later switches to NoSQL
items.explanation: A port shaped around SQL syntax has leaked its adapter's technology into the core's contract. The tell is exactly what's described: a fake in-memory adapter can't honestly satisfy that method without effectively becoming a tiny SQL engine.
items.reference:
✓ Port shape: written in the core's vocabulary
✗ Port shape dictated by an adapter's convenience

Why: if a port's shape depends on how one adapter works, the dependency has quietly flipped even though the arrow on the diagram still points inward.

items.prompt: Why is it a problem if a port's shape is 'dictated by what's convenient for Postgres,' even if every arrow on the architecture diagram still technically points inward?
choices: It's not a problem — arrow direction on the diagram is the only thing that matters

Because the diagram can lie: a port shaped around one adapter's needs has made the core implicitly depend on that adapter's assumptions, even while the drawn dependency arrow still points from adapter to port
It's only a problem for teams using more than one database
This situation is impossible to create by accident
items.explanation: The diagram shows the declared relationship, not the real one. A port whose shape only one adapter can naturally satisfy has smuggled that adapter's assumptions into the core, regardless of which way the arrow is drawn.
items.reference:
✓ Port shape: written in the core's vocabulary
✗ Port shape dictated by an adapter's convenience

Why: if a port's shape depends on how one adapter works, the dependency has quietly flipped even though the arrow on the diagram still points inward.

items.prompt: What is the 'composition root,' and why is it the one file allowed to know about both the core's ports and every concrete adapter?
choices: It's just another name for the core's main business logic file

It's the single place (e.g. `bootstrap.ts`) where concrete adapters are constructed and handed to the core — its only job is introducing the two sides to each other, so it's the one place allowed to know both
It's a build tool that auto-generates adapters
It's a folder name, not an actual file with logic in it
items.explanation: The composition root is where wiring happens: it constructs concrete adapters and passes them into the core's constructors. Because its entire purpose is introducing core and adapters to each other, it's the one place that legitimately needs to know both.
items.reference:
🧩 One file wires core + concrete adapters together
🔄 Swapping an adapter changes only that file

Why: if adapter construction were scattered through the codebase, a swap would mean hunting down every call site instead of editing one place.

items.prompt: Why does it matter that adapter construction (`new PostgresOrderRepository(...)`) happens in exactly one place, instead of wherever it's needed throughout the codebase?
choices: It doesn't matter — construction location is purely stylistic
Because a swap (Postgres to DynamoDB, or a real adapter to a test fake) then only requires editing one place — if construction were scattered, the same swap would mean hunting down every call site
Because JavaScript requires all constructors to be called from a single file
Because only one adapter instance is allowed to exist in the entire program
items.explanation: Centralizing construction is what makes a swap cheap. If `new PostgresOrderRepository(...)` appeared in a dozen places, switching adapters would mean finding and changing every one of them instead of one line in the composition root.
items.reference:
🧩 One file wires core + concrete adapters together
🔄 Swapping an adapter changes only that file

Why: if adapter construction were scattered through the codebase, a swap would mean hunting down every call site instead of editing one place.

items.prompt: What's a concrete, checkable signal that a port has leaked its adapter's shape into the core?
choices: The port has more than three methods

An honest, real implementation using a different technology (e.g. an in-memory fake) can't satisfy the port's contract without reimplementing pieces of the original adapter's technology (like a SQL parser)
The port interface is defined in a separate file from the core's use cases
The adapter class name doesn't match the port's name
items.explanation: If a fake adapter can't be written honestly — meaning it would have to embed something like a SQL interpreter just to satisfy a method signature — that's the concrete tell the port was shaped around one specific technology instead of the core's actual need.
items.reference:
🚩 Signal: an honest in-memory fake can't satisfy the port without reimplementing the adapter's tech

Why: a port that takes a raw SQL fragment, for example, has leaked Postgres's shape into the core's contract.

items.prompt: Testability usually breaks first when a port leaks its adapter's shape. Why testability specifically?
choices: Because tests are unrelated to port design
Because writing a second, honest implementation (like an in-memory fake, which tests rely on) is exactly the moment a port's technology-specific shape becomes impossible to satisfy cleanly
Because testability issues are always caused by slow test runners, not port design
Testability doesn't actually reveal this problem; only production incidents do
items.explanation: The in-memory fake used for fast tests is usually the second real implementation of a port a team writes — and it's exactly there that a technology-specific port shape (like a raw SQL parameter) becomes impossible to satisfy without absurd workarounds.
items.reference:
🚩 Signal: an honest in-memory fake can't satisfy the port without reimplementing the adapter's tech

Why: a port that takes a raw SQL fragment, for example, has leaked Postgres's shape into the core's contract.

items.prompt: In the worked example, `PlaceOrderUseCase` imports only `OrderRepository`, `StockChecker`, and language built-ins. What's a real, mechanical way to check a codebase actually follows this rule, not just claims to?
choices: Read the README to see what the team intended
Grep the core's files for `import` statements and check that every result is either a port the core defines or a language built-in — never a package like `pg` or `express`
Count the number of files in the core folder
Ask the original author whether they followed the pattern
items.explanation: This is a real, repeatable check: grep every core-layer file for `import`, and verify every hit is either one of the core's own ports or a language/runtime built-in. A single `import { Pool } from "pg"` in a use-case file is the pattern already broken, regardless of what the folder is named.
items.reference:
🔍 grep the core for import → only ports + language built-ins should show up

Why: a stray import { Pool } from "pg" inside a use-case file is the pattern already broken, no matter what the folder is named.

items.prompt: A teammate says their use-case file is 'clean' because it lives in a folder named `core/`. What's missing from that claim?
choices: Nothing — folder location is sufficient proof
Folder naming is cosmetic; the actual test is what the file imports — a file in `core/` can still directly import a database driver, and the folder name won't stop it or reveal it
The claim is correct as long as the folder also has a README
This only matters for TypeScript projects, not JavaScript
items.explanation: Folder structure doesn't enforce anything by itself — only the actual import graph does. A file sitting in `core/` while importing `pg` directly has violated the pattern regardless of where it's stored.
items.reference:
🔍 grep the core for import → only ports + language built-ins should show up

Why: a stray import { Pool } from "pg" inside a use-case file is the pattern already broken, no matter what the folder is named.

items.prompt: Implement `createInMemoryOrderRepository()`: `save(order)` stores a deep-enough copy of the order keyed by `order.id` (mutating the object passed to `save` afterward must not affect what's stored), and `findById(id)` returns the stored order, or `null` if nothing was saved under that id.

tests.description: returns null for an unknown id

tests.expr: (() => { const repo = createInMemoryOrderRepository(); repo.save({ id: 'o1', lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 2 }] }); return expect(repo.findById('o1')).toEqual({ id: 'o1', lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 2 }] }); })()

tests.description: mutating the original object after save() doesn't affect the stored copy
tests.expr: (() => { const repo = createInMemoryOrderRepository(); const order = { id: 'o1', lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 2 }] }; repo.save(order); order.lines.push({ sku: 'B', qty: 1 }); return expect(repo.findById('o1')).toEqual({ id: 'o1', lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 2 }] }); })()

items.explanation: The repository is a plain Map behind the same OrderRepository shape a Postgres adapter would implement. Copying the lines array on save (rather than storing the same reference) is what makes the fake honest — without it, a caller mutating their local order object after saving would silently corrupt what the 'database' has stored, a bug a real database could never have.
items.reference:
♻️ Same interface, two implementations: Postgres, in-memory
📄 The use case's own file never changes

Why: the use case's constructor only ever names the port type, never a concrete adapter class.

items.prompt: Implement `createInMemoryOrderRepository()`'s `save` to upsert by id (a second `save()` with the same id replaces the stored order, it doesn't create a duplicate), and `findById` to return `null` for anything never saved.

tests.description: saving twice with the same id updates, not duplicates
tests.expr: (() => { const repo = createInMemoryOrderRepository(); repo.save({ id: 'o1', lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 1 }] }); repo.save({ id: 'o1', lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 5 }] }); return expect(repo.findById('o1')).toEqual({ id: 'o1', lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 5 }] }); })()

(() => { const repo = createInMemoryOrderRepository(); repo.save({ id: 'o1', lines: [] }); repo.save({ id: 'o2', lines: [{ sku: 'B', qty: 1 }] }); return expect(repo.findById('o1')).toEqual({ id: 'o1', lines: [] }); })()

items.explanation: Map.set() with the same key naturally upserts, which is exactly what the Postgres adapter's `ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE` does too — the two adapters need to agree on this behavior, or a test passing against one would fail against the other, defeating the point of the shared contract.
items.reference:
♻️ Same interface, two implementations: Postgres, in-memory
📄 The use case's own file never changes

Why: the use case's constructor only ever names the port type, never a concrete adapter class.

items.prompt: A five-endpoint CRUD app has no business rules beyond field validation. Is introducing a port/adapter split for its single database table worth it?
choices: Yes, always — the pattern should be applied to every codebase regardless of size
Usually not — a port with exactly one adapter, forever, adds a file and a level of indirection while returning nothing, since there's no second implementation or real business rule to protect
Only if the app uses TypeScript
Only if more than 3 developers work on it
items.explanation: The pattern earns its cost when there's a real business rule to isolate, or a genuine second adapter (a test fake counts) to swap in. A CRUD app with neither is paying for an interface and a composition root with nothing to show for it.
items.reference:
Real business rulesworth it
5-endpoint CRUD, no rules yetusually not
Throwaway prototypenot yet

Why: a port with exactly one adapter, forever, pays a real cost (a file, a layer of indirection) for a swap that never happens.

items.prompt: What's the single-sentence version of the over-abstraction risk with ports & adapters?
choices: Interfaces are always a code smell in any language

A port with exactly one adapter, forever, is an interface that costs a file and a level of indirection while returning nothing — it only pays for itself once a second real implementation exists or is genuinely coming
Ports & adapters should never be used with SQL databases
The pattern is free as long as the team is experienced
items.explanation: The cost (a port file, a level of indirection, a composition root entry) is real and constant. The benefit only shows up once there's an actual second implementation — a real one, or a test double — to swap in. Zero second implementations means zero realized benefit.
items.reference:
Real business rulesworth it
5-endpoint CRUD, no rules yetusually not
Throwaway prototypenot yet

Why: a port with exactly one adapter, forever, pays a real cost (a file, a layer of indirection) for a swap that never happens.

items.prompt: A throwaway prototype that will likely be discarded within a month is being built. Per the trade-off table, should it get the port/adapter treatment now?
choices: Yes — always set up the full pattern from the first commit
Not yet — add the seam once real business logic (or the actual pain of testing it) shows up, not speculatively ahead of that need
No — prototypes should never use interfaces of any kind
Only if the prototype uses more than one database
items.explanation: The guidance is to add the seam when the pain (real business rules needing isolation, or genuinely painful tests) actually appears — not preemptively on a prototype that may never reach that point at all.
items.reference:
Real business rulesworth it
5-endpoint CRUD, no rules yetusually not
Throwaway prototypenot yet

Why: a port with exactly one adapter, forever, pays a real cost (a file, a layer of indirection) for a swap that never happens.

items.prompt: Implement `saveOrder(adapter, order)`: call `adapter.save(order)`. If the adapter throws an error whose `.code` is `'23505'` (Postgres's unique-violation code), catch it and throw a plain `Error` with the message `'duplicate order id'` instead of letting the original error escape. Any other thrown error should propagate unchanged.

tests.description: a unique-violation error is translated to a generic message
tests.expr: (() => { const badAdapter = { save() { const e = new Error('duplicate key value violates unique constraint'); e.code = '23505'; throw e; } }; let caught; try { saveOrder(badAdapter, { id: 'o1' }); } catch (e) { caught = e; } return expect(caught.message).toBe('duplicate order id'); })()
(() => { const okAdapter = { save() { return; } }; let threw = false; try { saveOrder(okAdapter, { id: 'o1' }); } catch { threw = true; } return expect(threw).toBe(false); })()

(() => { const otherAdapter = { save() { const e = new Error('connection refused'); e.code = 'ECONNREFUSED'; throw e; } }; let caught; try { saveOrder(otherAdapter, { id: 'o1' }); } catch (e) { caught = e; } return expect(caught.message).toBe('connection refused'); })()

items.explanation: The adapter is the only place that knows a '23505' code means 'unique violation' — that's Postgres-specific knowledge. Translating it into a generic error at the adapter boundary means the core (and its tests) never need to know Postgres error codes exist; letting other errors propagate unchanged avoids silently swallowing genuinely different failures.
items.reference:
📥 pg's UniqueViolationError leaks through the port unchanged

items.prompt: Implement `findOrderSafely(adapter, id)`: call `adapter.findById(id)` and return its result. If the adapter throws any error at all, catch it and return `null` instead of letting the failure propagate (treat 'couldn't reach storage' the same as 'not found' for this specific helper).

tests.description: returns the found order when the adapter succeeds
tests.expr: (() => { const adapter = { findById: () => ({ id: 'o1', lines: [] }) }; return expect(findOrderSafely(adapter, 'o1')).toEqual({ id: 'o1', lines: [] }); })()

tests.description: returns null when the adapter throws
tests.expr: (() => { const adapter = { findById: () => { throw new Error('timeout'); } }; return expect(findOrderSafely(adapter, 'o1')).toBe(null); })()

tests.description: returns null when the adapter itself returns null
tests.expr: (() => { const adapter = { findById: () => null }; return expect(findOrderSafely(adapter, 'missing')).toBe(null); })()

items.explanation: This helper deliberately collapses two different failure meanings ('not found' and 'storage unreachable') into one — a real design choice, and a debatable one, that's only safe to make explicitly and by-name (as a wrapper function), never silently inside the adapter itself where callers can't tell the two cases apart.

items.prompt: Both `PostgresOrderRepository` and `InMemoryOrderRepository` implement `OrderRepository`. Why isn't it enough to just unit-test the core against the in-memory one?
choices: It is enough — the Postgres adapter never needs its own tests

Because unit-testing the core only proves the rules are correct if the in-memory fake actually behaves like the real adapter — running the same contract test suite against both is what verifies that assumption
Because in-memory adapters are inherently unreliable and shouldn't be trusted at all
Because Postgres adapters never contain bugs
items.explanation: Testing the core against a fake only tells you the core is correct relative to that fake's behavior. If the fake has quietly drifted from the real adapter (e.g. it doesn't upsert by id the way Postgres's ON CONFLICT does), core tests would pass while production behaves differently — running the same contract tests against both adapters is what catches that.
items.reference:
🧪 Same test suite, run against BOTH adapters
⚠️ Otherwise a fake can silently drift from real behavior

Why: unit-testing the core with a fake only proves the rules are right if the fake still behaves like production.

items.prompt: A team simplifies `InMemoryOrderRepository.save()` to always insert instead of upserting by id, to save a line of code. What's the risk, even though all the core's unit tests still pass?
choices: No risk — if the tests pass, the behavior is correct

The fake now diverges from the real Postgres adapter's upsert behavior, so tests are validating the core against a repository that no longer matches production — a bug in this exact area could ship undetected
This only matters if the team also changes the Postgres adapter
In-memory adapters are not allowed to have any bugs by definition
items.explanation: Passing unit tests only prove the core behaves correctly against whatever the fake actually does — if the fake has silently diverged from the real adapter's contract, that's a gap contract tests are designed to catch, and plain unit tests against the fake alone will not.

Why: unit-testing the core with a fake only proves the rules are right if the fake still behaves like production.

items.prompt: `placeOrder()` needs to save the order AND decrement stock atomically — if stock decrement fails, the order save must not stick either. `OrderRepository` and `StockChecker` are two separate ports today. What does the pattern give you for free here?
choices: Atomicity across two ports for free, automatically

Nothing automatic — spanning two separate ports atomically requires a deliberate new seam, such as a UnitOfWork port wrapping both operations, or collapsing them into one adapter with a single transaction
The pattern makes this scenario impossible to need
Only the Postgres adapter needs to worry about this, not the core
items.explanation: Ports & adapters gives you swappable, testable pieces — it does not give you cross-port atomicity automatically. That has to be designed deliberately, typically as a UnitOfWork-style port or by having one adapter own both operations inside a single database transaction.
items.reference:
🔗 Two ports, two separate commits → no atomicity by default
📦 Fix: a UnitOfWork port, or one adapter owning both operations in one transaction

Why: ports & adapters doesn't hand you atomicity across two ports for free — that has to be designed as its own seam.

items.prompt: If `StockChecker` were genuinely backed by a different system than `OrderRepository` (say, an external inventory API instead of the same database), what changes about achieving atomicity across the two?
choices: Nothing changes — atomicity is always achievable regardless of the systems involved

True atomicity may not be achievable at all across two different systems — the realistic fallback becomes a compensating action (undo the order save) if the second call fails, not a single guaranteed transaction
The two ports should be merged into one port that ignores the distinction
This scenario requires abandoning the ports & adapters pattern entirely
items.explanation: A single database transaction can span two tables in the same database, but it generally can't span two independent systems (a database and an external HTTP API). At that point the realistic tool is a compensating action — detect the partial failure and actively undo the first operation — not true atomicity.
items.reference:
🔗 Two ports, two separate commits → no atomicity by default
📦 Fix: a UnitOfWork port, or one adapter owning both operations in one transaction

Why: ports & adapters doesn't hand you atomicity across two ports for free — that has to be designed as its own seam.

items.prompt: What's the deciding factor in choosing between a UnitOfWork port versus collapsing two ports into one adapter with a single transaction, when an operation needs to span both?
choices: Whichever option requires fewer lines of code

Whether the two things being coordinated live in the same underlying technology (same database, collapsible into one transaction) or genuinely different systems (needing a coordinating seam like UnitOfWork, or a compensating action if true atomicity isn't available)
The choice is arbitrary and has no real consequence
UnitOfWork should always be preferred regardless of the situation
items.explanation: If both operations ultimately hit the same database, one adapter owning a single transaction is often simplest. If they're genuinely different systems, a UnitOfWork-style port (or accepting only a compensating action) is the honest way to model that coordination boundary explicitly.
